title: Indian Creator's Schengen Visa Rejected: The 3 Mistakes She Wants You to Avoid
excerpt: Garima Singh's rejection notice cited an unreliable itinerary, an uncertain purpose of stay and a name mismatch — three classic red flags behind India's 181,000 Schengen refusals last year.
body:
• Indian content creator Garima Singh shared a candid video revealing her Schengen visa was rejected, listing the three reasons on her rejection notice: an unreliable itinerary, an uncertain purpose of stay, and a name mismatch across her documents.
  • Her warning to followers: "Don't make the mistakes I made!"
  • The context is sobering: of the 1.15 million-plus Schengen applications filed by Indians in 2025, roughly 181,000 were rejected — a 15.8% refusal rate, above the 14.8% global average, according to European Commission data cited by Outlook Traveller.
  • Consulates differ sharply: Germany rejected about 10.5% of 153,000+ Indian applications, while Slovenia turned down nearly 47% and Greece about a third. Rejected applicants collectively lost an estimated Rs 125 crore in non-refundable fees.

An Indian content creator's visa rejection has become a cautionary tale for Europe-bound travellers. Garima Singh, posting a candid video for her followers, revealed that her Schengen visa was refused — and read out the three reasons stamped on her rejection notice.

"Don't make the mistakes I made!" she told viewers. "Teen reason mujhe mile hain. Pehla reason ye mila hai ki that your itinerary is not reliable." The three grounds: an itinerary the consulate found unreliable, an uncertain purpose of stay, and a name mismatch across her documents.

Why these three mistakes matter

Each of Singh's three reasons maps to a classic consular red flag. An itinerary that doesn't hold together — dates that don't match hotel bookings, gaps that can't be explained — undermines the entire application. A vague purpose of stay leaves the officer doubting what the trip is actually for. And a name mismatch, however minor, across a passport, application form and bookings raises questions about identity that no cover letter can easily fix.

Immigration experts consistently name the same cluster of refusal drivers: insufficient or inconsistent financial proof, weak evidence of ties to India or unclear return intent, incomplete documentation, vague travel purpose, travel-insurance errors, applying to the wrong consulate, and inconsistencies between documents. A bank statement that doesn't align with declared income, or an itinerary that doesn't match hotel bookings, can turn a routine submission into a refusal.

The numbers behind the rejections

Singh is far from alone. Indians filed more than 1.15 million Schengen applications in 2025, of which about 967,000 were issued and roughly 181,000 rejected — a 15.8% refusal rate against a 14.8% global average. The consulate you apply to matters enormously: Belgium approved more than 91% of Indian applications and Denmark over 90%, while Germany — despite processing over 153,000 Indian applications, one of the highest volumes in Europe — kept its rejection rate to around 10.5%. At the other end, Slovenia rejected nearly half of Indian applications, and Greece, despite being among the most popular European destinations for Indian travellers, turned down roughly a third.

The financial sting is real. The Schengen visa fee is 90 euros, non-refundable — and one analysis estimated Indians lost roughly Rs 125 crore in visa fees alone from rejected applications. Schengen rules also require travel insurance of at least 30,000 euros for medical emergencies; policies that fall short are another common tripwire.

"Don't make the mistakes I made!"

— Garima Singh, content creator

What to get right

The practical checklist writes itself from Singh's experience: keep the itinerary consistent and verifiable across every document; state a clear, specific purpose; make sure the name matches exactly across passport, application and bookings; show consistent financial proof; apply to the consulate of the country that is the trip's main destination; and carry compliant 30,000-euro travel insurance. None of it is glamorous — but as Singh's rejection shows, consulates read the paperwork before they read the person.
